newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds lower after U.S. rate hike signals.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds lower after U.S. rate hike signals.

text.p: Irish bonds trade was mixed as benign Irish inflation data was overshadowed by fears of a U.S. rate hike following words of warning by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan, dealers said.

"There was some short-end selling on the back of the CPI figures, which were much better than most of us expected, but later people retreated along with the rest of Europe after the Greenspan comments," a dealer said.
Interest rate jitters hit Wall Street shortly after the open when Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan signalled a possible rate rise at next week's U.S. policy-making session.

Greenspan warned that the economy retained a "great deal of vigour" and that a further drop in unemployment would increase the risk of higher wages and prices. He said the U.S. must act pre-emptively to keep inflation low.

Earlier the Irish February consumer price index showed a lower-than-expected rise of 0.6 percent month-on-month, giving a year-on-year increase of 1.5 percent. Forecasts ranged from a rise of up to 1.0 percent m/m and 2.0 percent y/y.
"This data is good news for the country," a dealer said. "It brings Ireland into line with the rest of the EU, and consistently-low inflation is good for investors and good for the market."
By mid-afternoon the spread on the Irish 10-year bond had narrowed to 101 basis points over Germany from an opening of 104, dealers said.

By 1610 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was unchanged from Tuesday's close at 100.75 to yield 6.29 percent while the benchmark eight percent bond due 2006 was down 10 pence from the close at 106.85 to yield 6.97 percent.
